planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring into constantly shaded, humus-rich soil and mulch with leaf litter to keep the shallow roots cool.

directions: Disporopsis longifolia is an evergreen rhizomatous perennial from subtropical woodlands of southern China and continental Southeast Asia, closely related to the more commonly grown Disporopsis pernyi but distinguished by noticeably narrower, elongated leaf blades. Arching stems carry small, dangling, bell-shaped cream flowers in spring followed by round berries that darken as they ripen. It spreads gradually by rhizome to form a low, glossy-leaved mat in constantly shaded, humus-rich soil, and in mild climates it holds its foliage through winter. Give it the same deep shade and leaf-litter mulch favored by other woodland Disporopsis species, and divide clumps in spring only when increase is wanted.

planting.note: Divide and plant in early spring into cool, deeply shaded, humus-rich soil, keeping divisions evenly moist until re-established.

directions: Chloranthus multistachys is a clump-forming woodland perennial from mid-elevation forests in central and southwestern China, grown for its glossy, coarsely toothed leaves and the unusual way each flowering stem produces several slender spikes of tiny, fragrant white flowers rather than the single spike typical of its relatives. It emerges in spring from a short rhizome and prefers the same cool, deeply shaded, humus-rich conditions as Chloranthus japonicus and Chloranthus serratus already grown in woodland gardens. The plant spreads slowly to form a modest colony over several seasons and resents disturbance once established. Divide in early spring if propagation is needed, keeping divisions consistently moist until re-established.

planting.note: Divide established clumps in spring or fall and plant into constantly shaded, humus-rich soil mulched with leaf litter.

directions: Asarum forbesii is a low, evergreen wild ginger from Chinese woodlands, forming a tight groundcover of heart-shaped leaves that are heavily mottled with silver-gray along the veins. Its small, maroon-brown, bell-shaped flowers are produced at ground level in spring, hidden beneath the foliage in the manner typical of the genus. Like other Asian Asarum species it spreads slowly by rhizome and performs best in constantly shaded, humus-rich soil that never dries out. Divide established clumps in spring or fall to propagate, and mulch with leaf litter to keep the shallow roots cool.

planting.note: Divide immediately after flowering in spring and plant into humus-rich, well-drained soil under deciduous trees.

directions: Hepatica transsilvanica is a woodland perennial native to forests of Romania and the surrounding Carpathian region, larger and more vigorous in growth than the familiar Hepatica nobilis. Rounded, softly lobed evergreen leaves persist through winter and are joined in earliest spring by lavender-blue flowers held just above the foliage, often appearing while snow is still nearby. It slowly forms an expanding clump in humus-rich, well-drained soil under deciduous trees, tolerating more open dappled shade than many other hepaticas. Division is best done immediately after flowering, since the fleshy roots resent disturbance once new growth is underway.

planting.note: Divide shallow rhizomes carefully in spring and plant into consistently moist, cool, humus-rich soil in deep shade.

directions: Streptopus streptopoides is a diminutive, creeping woodland perennial found in cool, moist forests from the Pacific Northwest and Alaska across to Japan, far smaller in every respect than the more commonly grown Streptopus amplexifolius. Thin, wiry stems carry small, rounded leaves and tiny purplish-pink, bell-shaped flowers that nod from the leaf axils in late spring, followed by translucent red berries. It spreads slowly by slender rhizomes into a low mat and demands consistently moist, cool, humus-rich soil in deep shade, struggling wherever summers turn hot or dry. Best propagated by careful division of the shallow rhizomes in spring, since seed-grown plants are slow to establish.

planting.note: Divide clumps in spring and plant into humus-rich, well-drained woodland-edge soil, avoiding overly rich or wet sites.

directions: Patrinia villosa is a woodland-edge perennial from Japan, Korea, and China, distinguished from the sun-loving golden Patrinia scabiosifolia by its preference for shaded sites and its clusters of small white, rather than yellow, flowers produced in late summer and fall. Softly hairy, toothed leaves form a modest clump that slowly increases from short rhizomes in humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil. It tolerates considerably more shade than most Patrinia relatives and combines well with ferns and other shade perennials at a woodland edge. Divide clumps in spring, and avoid overly rich or wet soil, which can cause lax, floppy growth.
